title: The Latin Square With Greater-Than Signs

concept.title: The same search as the Latin square, with one more rule for every sign
body: In a *futoshiki* puzzle you fill an `n` by `n` grid with the numbers `1 .. n`, each once per row and column, and some neighbouring cells carry a **less-than sign** between them: the number in one cell must be smaller than the number in the other. Some cells may be given. We count the solutions.

The search is the one of the Latin square: bit masks for the used numbers of every row and column, and the empty cell with the fewest candidates first. The new rule is added to the candidates of a cell: for each sign that links the cell with a **neighbour that has a number already**, only the numbers that keep the sign true are allowed. If the neighbour must be bigger than this cell and has the number `v`, the cell may only take numbers from `1` to `v - 1`; if it must be smaller, from `v + 1` to `n`.

A sign between two **given** cells is checked once at the start; if it is false the answer is 0. As before, given numbers that repeat in a row or a column also give 0. With at least eight clues in total (given numbers and signs) the search is tiny.

statement: An `n` by `n` grid is partly filled with numbers 1 to `n` (empty cells are `0`). There are `m` signs: each says that the number in a cell must be smaller than the number in a neighbouring cell (they share a side). Count the ways to fill the empty cells so that every row and every column has each of the numbers 1 to `n` exactly once and all signs are true. If the given numbers already break a rule, the answer is 0.
inputFormat: The next `n` lines have `n` characters each (digits 0 to `n`, no spaces).
The next `m` lines each have four numbers `r1 c1 r2 c2` (rows and columns from 1): the number at `(r1, c1)` must be smaller than the number at `(r2, c2)`.
constraints: The two cells of a sign share a side.
If n is 5, the number of given cells plus m is at least 8.

examples.note: A 3 by 3 puzzle with four signs and no given numbers.

hints: Use the bit masks of the Latin square and the cell with the fewest candidates.
For every sign, remove from the candidates of a cell the numbers that would break it, when the other cell already has a number.
Check signs between two given numbers at the start.

explanation: Bit masks for rows and columns give the basic candidates; every sign to a neighbour that already has a number trims the candidates to the numbers below or above it. The search takes the cell with the fewest candidates; contradictions among the givens (repeats or false signs) give 0.
solution.complexity: Time small with eight or more clues, space O(n^2).
